# 90-Day ISO 27001 Readiness Plan for a Mid-Sized SaaS Company

Based on your profile, you're in reasonable shape operationally but missing the ISMS "paper trail" and a few critical controls (PAM, consistent patching, risk assessment). Here's a prioritized plan.

## Guiding principles

Auditors assess two things: that your ISMS exists as a managed system (Clauses 4–10), and that your Annex A controls are implemented or justifiably excluded. For a 90-day push to readiness (not certification itself, which typically takes 6–12 months with a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit), focus on building the ISMS skeleton, closing your highest-risk control gaps, and generating 2–3 months of operational evidence before Stage 1.

## Days 1–30: Foundation and Scoping

The goal this month is to establish governance, define scope, and start the risk assessment. Without these, nothing else counts as ISMS evidence.

| # | Task | Annex A / Clause | Owner | Quick-win evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Appoint ISMS owner and steering committee; document roles | Clause 5.3, A.5.2 | CTO or CISO | Signed roles-and-responsibilities doc, steering committee charter, meeting minutes |
| 2 | Define ISMS scope (SaaS product, supporting infra, corp IT) | Clause 4.3 | ISMS owner | Scope statement signed by leadership |
| 3 | Draft Information Security Policy | Clause 5.2, A.5.1 | CISO / ISMS owner | Policy document, leadership approval, communication record |
| 4 | Identify interested parties and legal/contractual requirements | Clause 4.2, A.5.31 | Legal + ISMS owner | Register of interested parties, compliance obligations register |
| 5 | Build asset inventory (fix CMDB gaps for in-scope systems) | A.5.9, A.5.12 | IT manager | Asset register with owners and classification |
| 6 | Define risk assessment methodology | Clause 6.1.2 | ISMS owner | Risk methodology document |
| 7 | Run initial risk assessment workshop | Clause 6.1.2 | ISMS owner + tech leads | Risk register (draft) |
| 8 | Document supplier list and criticality (AWS, payments, analytics) | A.5.19–5.22 | Procurement / IT manager | Supplier register with risk ratings |

**Top quick wins this month**: the scope statement, information security policy, asset register, and initial risk register. These four documents anchor everything else.

## Days 31–60: Close critical control gaps

This is where you address your known weaknesses. I'd prioritize PAM, patching, and access provisioning because they're the controls most likely to generate audit findings and real breaches.

| # | Task | Annex A | Owner | Quick-win evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | Implement PAM or at minimum vaulted admin credentials for AWS and prod | A.8.2, A.5.15 | IT manager / DevOps lead | PAM tool config, list of privileged accounts, access logs |
| 10 | Formalize access provisioning: joiner/mover/leaver workflow with approvals | A.5.16, A.5.18 | IT manager + HR | JML procedure, ticket evidence, quarterly access review records |
| 11 | Enforce MFA everywhere (AWS, SaaS admin consoles, corp SSO, VPN) | A.8.5 | IT manager | MFA policy, configuration screenshots, coverage report |
| 12 | Patching standard: define SLAs by severity, assign owners | A.8.8 | IT manager / DevOps | Patch management procedure, vuln scan reports, remediation tickets |
| 13 | Enforce change management for all production changes (not just "usually") | A.8.32 | Change manager | Updated change policy, CAB minutes, change tickets with approvals |
| 14 | Secure development practices (SDLC, code review, SAST) | A.8.25–8.29 | Engineering lead | SDLC policy, PR review records, SAST tool reports |
| 15 | Risk treatment plan: decide accept/mitigate/transfer for each top risk | Clause 6.1.3 | ISMS owner | Risk treatment plan, Statement of Applicability (draft) |
| 16 | Supplier security review process (questionnaires, SOC 2 collection) | A.5.19–5.22 | Procurement / CISO | Supplier assessments, AWS shared responsibility matrix, SOC 2 reports on file |
| 17 | Incident response: formalize classification, escalation, evidence handling | A.5.24–5.28 | Incident manager | IR plan, runbooks, post-incident reviews |

**Top quick wins this month**: PAM deployment, universal MFA, documented patching SLAs with evidence of adherence, and completed risk treatment plan with draft SoA.

## Days 61–90: Operational evidence and readiness

Auditors want to see the ISMS running, not just documented. This month is about generating repeated evidence of operation.

| # | Task | Annex A / Clause | Owner | Quick-win evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | Finalize Statement of Applicability (all 93 Annex A controls) | Clause 6.1.3 | ISMS owner | SoA with justifications |
| 19 | Backup restoration test with documented results | A.8.13 | IT manager | Test plan, restore logs, sign-off |
| 20 | Business continuity and disaster recovery test (tabletop minimum) | A.5.29, A.5.30 | ISMS owner + IT | BCP/DRP documents, tabletop exercise report |
| 21 | Security awareness training rollout and tracking | A.6.3 | HR + CISO | Training platform records, completion rates, phishing sim results |
| 22 | Logging and monitoring: ensure coverage of critical systems, define alerts | A.8.15, A.8.16 | DevOps / SecOps | Logging architecture doc, sample alerts, SIEM dashboards |
| 23 | Cryptography and key management policy (encryption at rest/in transit) | A.8.24 | Engineering lead | Crypto policy, AWS KMS config, TLS inventory |
| 24 | Data classification and handling procedures | A.5.12, A.5.13 | ISMS owner | Classification scheme, handling guide, examples applied |
| 25 | Internal audit of the ISMS | Clause 9.2 | Independent reviewer | Audit plan, findings report, corrective actions |
| 26 | Management review meeting | Clause 9.3 | ISMS owner + leadership | Agenda, minutes, decisions, action items |
| 27 | First quarterly access review executed | A.5.18 | IT manager | Review records with evidence of revocations |
| 28 | Metrics and KPIs dashboard (incidents, patch SLA, training completion) | Clause 9.1 | ISMS owner | Dashboard, trend data |

**Top quick wins this month**: successful restore test, management review minutes, internal audit report, and a metrics dashboard showing the ISMS is being actively managed.

## Highest-priority Annex A controls to implement first

If you can only focus on ten controls in the first 90 days given your current state, I'd pick:

A.5.15 Access control, A.5.18 Access rights (your ad-hoc provisioning is the biggest finding risk), A.8.2 Privileged access (no PAM is a serious gap), A.8.5 Authentication (MFA everywhere), A.8.8 Vulnerability management (inconsistent patching), A.8.32 Change management (process exists but not followed), A.5.19–5.22 Supplier security (multiple third parties), A.5.24 Incident management (formalize what you already do well), A.8.13 Backup (add consistent restore testing), and A.5.9 Asset management (close CMDB gaps).

## Evidence collection tips

Auditors love artifacts that prove a process ran repeatedly: ticket exports showing change approvals over time, access review spreadsheets with sign-offs, patch compliance reports month-over-month, training completion dashboards, and incident post-mortems. Start collecting these from day one even if the processes aren't perfect yet. Three months of imperfect-but-documented evidence beats one month of polished evidence.

## Things to flag to leadership

Three realities worth setting expectations on now: certification itself likely takes 6–12 months, not 90 days, because Stage 2 auditors want to see 2–3 months of ISMS operation. You'll need budget for an accredited certification body (typically $15–40k for a company your size, plus annual surveillance audits), and possibly a PAM tool and GRC platform. And someone needs real ownership: a part-time ISMS owner with a full workload usually leads to a stalled program.

Want me to go deeper on any section, draft specific policy templates, or sketch out what the Statement of Applicability should look like for your environment?
